etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English awaiten, from Old Northern French awaitier (“to lie in wait for, watch, observe”), originally especially with a hostile sense; itself from a- (“to”) + waitier (“to watch”). More at English wait.

quote.citation: 1674, John Milton, “Book IV”, in Paradise Lost:
quote.text: Betwixt these rocky pillars Gabriel sat, / Chief of the angelic guards, awaiting night;

quote.citation: 1897 December (indicated as 1898), Winston Churchill, chapter II, in The Celebrity: An Episode, New York, N.Y.: The Macmillan Company; London: Macmillan & Co., Ltd., →OCLC:
quote.text: I had occasion […] to make a somewhat long business trip to Chicago, and on my return […] I found Farrar awaiting me in the railway station. He smiled his wonted fraction by way of greeting, […], and finally leading me to his buggy, turned and drove out of town.

quote.citation: 2024 April 17, “Rural railways: do they deliver?”, in RAIL, number 1007, page 57:
quote.text: After 170416 heads into the bay platform (2) to be prepared for its next trip to 'Skeggy', there's time to grab a coffee and await the arrival of RAIL's next train - the 1144 Leicester-Grimsby Town.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To be in store for; to be ready or in waiting for.

quote.citation: 1900, Charles W. Chesnutt, chapter I, in The House Behind the Cedars:
quote.text: Standing foursquare in the heart of the town, at the intersection of the two main streets, a "jog" at each street corner left around the market-house a little public square, which at this hour was well occupied by carts and wagons from the country and empty drays awaiting hire.

quote.citation: 1674, John Milton, “Book XI”, in Paradise Lost:
quote.text: O Eve, some further change awaits us nigh.

definitions.definition: (transitive, intransitive) To serve or attend; to wait on, wait upon.
(intransitive) To wait; to stay in waiting.
